solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A piece of luggage short on vehicle reaching capital

indicators.note: something cut short has lost its final part, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: a car is a vehicle
taken as written
a case is a suitcase, a piece of luggage

explanation.surface: A traveller's suitcase is too small for the car taking them to the city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A piece of luggage' looks like one item, but the A stands alone; in an across answer 'on' means placed after.
explanation.definitionFit: Caracas is the capital city of Venezuela, so it is an example of a capital.

clue.text: Roughly 50cm frame for Spain’s top artist

indicators.note: a frame surrounds a picture, so one piece goes round the other
the top of a word written down is its opening letter

blocks.note: the cubit, an ancient forearm-length measure, is about half a metre
the first letter of Spain

explanation.surface: A picture frame about half a metre wide for the best painter in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: The 50cm is not a frame size but a unit: a cubit was the length from elbow to fingertip, roughly half a metre.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cubist is a painter of the Cubist movement, like Picasso or Braque, so an example of an artist.

clue.text: Soldier not smelling so good

blocks.note: first meaning: a soldier serving in the ranks rather than as an officer
second meaning: comparative of rank, meaning foul-smelling

explanation.surface: A sweaty private on manoeuvres is a little whiffy.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one soldier who needs a wash; it is two separate senses of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: A ranker is an enlisted private; rank also means stinking, and adding -er gives the comparative form.

clue.text: Vehement Conservative originally lacking in love

indicators.note: what something was originally is how it began, so only its opening letter counts

blocks.note: C is the standard abbreviation for Conservative
the first letter of lacking
amorous means in love

explanation.surface: A fiery Tory politician who at first had no romantic feelings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lacking in love' reads as one phrase, but it splits: 'originally lacking' is one letter and 'in love' is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Clamorous means noisily insistent, and a vehement protest is loud and forceful in the same way.

clue.text: Brickie could use this degree of enthusiasm

blocks.note: first meaning: a bubble tool for checking a surface is horizontal
second meaning, read literally: how high one's spirit or zest is

explanation.walkthrough: A brickie is a bricklayer, British slang. The second half splits the phrase back into its words: spirit is enthusiasm and level is degree.
explanation.definitionFit: Bricklayers check each course is true with the bubble tool; and the amount of one's vim is literally its level.

clue.text: Unsatisfactory part of process withdrawn from view

blocks.note: behaviour that is off is unacceptable
a stage is one step in a process

explanation.surface: A faulty step in some procedure has been hidden from sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's a bit off' is British for 'that's not acceptable', which is the sense used here.
explanation.definitionFit: Actors who go off-stage leave the audience's sight, so the term means hidden or out of public sight.

clue.text: Scorer from cricket side Queen’s invested in

indicators.note: to be invested in something is to be placed inside it, as money is put into a business

blocks.note: the off side is one half of a cricket field
R for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: A run-maker from a cricket team that the monarch has put money into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scorer' suggests a batsman, but it is someone who writes scores: a composer. Carl Orff wrote Carmina Burana.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical score is a written composition, so a scorer is a composer such as Orff.

clue.text: Material in soft soap better with edges trimmed

indicators.note: trimming the edges cuts off both ends, so the first and last letters drop

blocks.note: flannel is British slang for smooth, flattering talk
taken as written before trimming

explanation.surface: A cloth soaked in gentle soap, better once its frayed edges are cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soft soap' is not soap but flattery; flannel is the British word for the same smooth talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Flannelette is a soft brushed cotton cloth used for sheets and nightwear, so it is a kind of fabric.

clue.text: Feel affronted & decamp from ‘ere

blocks.note: to take off is to leave in a hurry
'from here' is hence, and the apostrophe drops the H as a Cockney speaker would

explanation.surface: Someone insulted storms off, told in Cockney to clear out of here.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'ere marks a dropped H, so 'from 'ere' is hence without its H.
explanation.definitionFit: To be affronted is to be insulted, and taking offence is the idiom for feeling hurt or resentful at it.

clue.text: Pig finally produced her young, and looked brilliant

indicators.note: what comes finally comes at the end, so only the closing letter is kept

blocks.note: the last letter of pig
a sow that littered gave birth to a litter

explanation.surface: A sow gives birth at last and looks radiant.
explanation.walkthrough: The sow seems to be the subject of the whole sentence, but the pig only gives its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To glitter is to sparkle with light, so the past tense means shone or looked dazzling.

clue.text: Farm assistant to remain on far side of pass

indicators.note: being on the far side means coming beyond, so this piece is written after the other

blocks.note: a col is a mountain pass
to lie is to stay or remain in place

explanation.surface: A farmhand is told to stay on the other side of the mountain pass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On far side of' places the remaining piece after the pass. A col is the low point of a ridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Collies are sheepdogs used to herd flocks, so the dog is a helper working on a farm.

clue.text: Bring down public drink dispenser

blocks.note: overt means open, done in public
a tea urn dispenses hot drinks

explanation.surface: Knock over the communal water cooler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Public drink dispenser' reads as one object, but 'public' is a separate adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: To overturn a government or ruling is to topple it, which is what bringing it down means.

clue.text: Bar number?

blocks.note: surface reading: a song sung or a figure on a bill in a pub
setter's reading: the bar is a neighbourhood pub, and a number is something that numbs

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain the local is your nearby pub, so 'bar' gives the first word; 'number' is read as numb-er, a thing that numbs.
explanation.definitionFit: A drug that deadens feeling in one area is a numbing agent, and its name puns on the pub word.

clue.text: How Roman Briton might announce 10p charge?

indicators.note: announcing is saying out loud, and a Roman would write the number ten as a letter

blocks.note: ten in Roman numerals is X, and p stands for pence

explanation.surface: A Briton under Roman rule calls out a price of ten pence.
explanation.walkthrough: The Roman Briton writes 10 as X, so '10p' is spoken 'ex pence'.
explanation.definitionFit: An expense is a cost or outlay, and a charge is the price asked for something.

clue.text: US diplomat, one with a tale after hold-up in W African state

indicators.note: being in a place means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other
coming after means following, so this piece is written later in the answer

blocks.note: Benin is a country in West Africa
a traffic jam is a hold-up
the Franklin is a pilgrim who tells a story in Chaucer's Canterbury Tales

explanation.surface: An American envoy with a story to tell after being delayed in West Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One with a tale' points to Chaucer: a franklin was a medieval landowner, and The Franklin's Tale is one of the Canterbury Tales.
explanation.definitionFit: The founding father served as American envoy to France, negotiating the 1778 alliance, so he was a statesman abroad.

clue.text: Spooner’s leading ram providing part of service?

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of neighbouring words

blocks.note: key means leading or main; it takes the T sound from the other word
a tup is a ram; it takes the K sound from the other word

explanation.surface: A lead ram supplying something for a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: A tup is a dialect word for a ram. 'Service' looks like a church service, but it is a tea service.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea service is a matching set of crockery, and each cup in it is one piece of the set.

clue.text: Team considers talking obliquely

indicators.note: talking means speaking, so the word is heard rather than read

blocks.note: a side is a team
to weigh something up is to consider it

explanation.surface: A squad weighs up its options while speaking indirectly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Talking obliquely' reads as one phrase, but 'talking' belongs to the wordplay and 'obliquely' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done obliquely is slanting or indirect, and moving sideways is moving at an angle rather than straight.

clue.text: Contrary flyers, admitting lack of exercise, get going

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so one piece takes the other inside it
contrary means going the opposite way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: tits are small songbirds
no PE: PE is physical education at school

explanation.surface: Awkward birds that have not been exercised need to get a move on.
explanation.walkthrough: PE is physical education, so 'lack of exercise' is NO PE. The birds go round it first, then the whole string turns back.
explanation.definitionFit: Step on it is an idiom for hurry up, from pressing the accelerator pedal, so it urges someone to move.

clue.text: Hamish’s very puny Scot ignoring outsiders

indicators.note: the outsiders of a word are its first and last letters, and these are left out

blocks.note: taken as written before losing its ends
taken as written before losing its ends

explanation.surface: A Highlander named Hamish describes a feeble fellow Scot.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamish is a typical Scottish name, so 'Hamish's very' asks for the Scots word meaning very.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots dialect unco is an adverb meaning extremely or remarkably, used as very is in English.

clue.text: Test cricket side hosting extremely tough event

indicators.note: a host has guests inside their home, so one piece holds another
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only first and last letters stay

blocks.note: a trial is a test
the outer letters of tough
the on side is one half of a cricket field

explanation.surface: A Test match team is hosting a very hard fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Test cricket' wants to be one phrase, a Test being an international match; here 'Test' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A triathlon is a sporting contest of swimming, cycling and running, so it is a competition in an athletics programme.

clue.text: He wrote about cutting grass before church

indicators.note: cutting into something means entering its middle, so one piece sits inside
coming before means preceding, so the next piece follows

blocks.note: a lawn is an area of grass
re means about or concerning
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A man wrote about mowing the lawn before going to church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting grass' suggests mowing, but 'cutting' is the piece going into the grass. 'He wrote' defines any author, here D. H. Lawrence.
explanation.definitionFit: D. H. Lawrence was an English novelist, author of Sons and Lovers, so he is a man who wrote.

clue.text: Go round with bell – a normal start to school day

definitions.text: a normal start to school day

blocks.note: to roll is to turn round and round
in British slang, to give someone a bell is to phone them, a call

explanation.surface: A school bell rings and children go round to start the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give me a bell' is everyday British for 'phone me', so a bell is a call.
explanation.definitionFit: A roll call is the reading of names to check attendance, the routine register at the opening of lessons.

clue.text: A carbon-free supply, showing restraint

indicators.note: read as the adverb of supple, it means bendily, so the letters are bent out of shape

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A green energy supply that shows self-control on emissions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like a noun, but it is the adverb from supple, spoken sup-lee. 'Carbon-free' seems to remove a C, yet the C stays in.
explanation.definitionFit: Forbearance is patient self-control, holding back from acting, which is what restraint means.

clue.text: Resetting carpals round tip of ulna’s become a bit of a habit

indicators.note: resetting a broken bone moves pieces into new positions, so the letters are rearranged
going round something means surrounding it, so one piece encloses another
the tip of something is its very first point, so only the opening letter is used

blocks.note: taken as written
the first letter of ulna

explanation.surface: A surgeon setting wrist bones around the forearm keeps doing it out of routine.
explanation.walkthrough: Carpals and ulna make this look medical, and the scapula is a bone too, but 'habit' is a monk's robe, not a routine.
explanation.definitionFit: A scapular is a long strip of cloth worn over the shoulders as part of a monk's or nun's robe.

clue.text: Cover core of talks during European exit

indicators.note: the core is the very centre, so only the middle letter is kept
what happens during something falls within it, so one piece sits inside

blocks.note: to the British, continental means from mainland Europe
to quit is to leave
the middle letter of talks

explanation.surface: Hiding what was really said in the negotiations over Brexit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'European exit' sounds like Brexit talks, but it splits into an adjective and a verb. A continental quilt is an older British name for a duvet.
explanation.definitionFit: A duvet is a padded bedspread, so it is a covering for a bed, which is what cover means here.

clue.text: Snappy series of deliveries in mixed styles

blocks.note: someone snappy is irritable, cross
in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled

explanation.surface: A sharp-tongued postman's rounds mixing up different ways of working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deliveries' suggests the post, but in cricket a delivery is a ball bowled, and six make an over.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossover is music or art blending genres, such as a classical singer recording pop, so it combines different genres.

clue.text: Unsettled on defeat, not appreciating ups and downs

indicators.note: unsettled means disturbed from its proper order, so the letters move

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Shaken by losing, a player who never values life's highs and lows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ups and downs' sounds like fortune, but here it means rising and falling notes in a tune.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone tone-deaf cannot tell differences in musical pitch, so they miss a melody's rises and falls.

clue.text: Ablaze, always full of this enthusiasm

indicators.note: full of means containing, so the letters are sitting inside the words before

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone constantly on fire with keenness.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma between the two words does not stop the run of letters across them.
explanation.definitionFit: Zeal is fervent eagerness for a cause, so it is a strong form of enthusiasm.

clue.text: Soundness I’d found in large university, Oxford for one

indicators.note: what is found in a place is located inside it, so one piece goes within

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for large, as on clothing
U is the abbreviation for university
Oxford is an example of a city
the contraction written without its apostrophe

explanation.surface: A student claims to have found good sense at a big university like Oxford.
explanation.walkthrough: 'University, Oxford' reads as one place, but the university gives only U and Oxford stands for any city.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucidity is clear-headed sanity, and soundness of mind means the same mental clarity.

clue.text: One Spartan character unknown by another

indicators.note: by means next to, so the two pieces sit side by side

blocks.note: in algebra x, y and z stand for unknown quantities
another Spartan character: eta, a different letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A tough Spartan figure is unknown to his comrade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spartan character' looks like a person of stern habits, but Sparta was Greek, so a character is a Greek letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Zeta is the sixth letter of the Greek alphabet, which the ancient Spartans used for writing.

clue.text: Mineral brew in ewer runs out

indicators.note: being in a vessel means held inside it, so one piece goes within
out means removed, so this letter is taken away

blocks.note: a ewer is a large water jug, a pitcher
a brew is a mixture, a blend
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Mineral water poured into a jug until it is empty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs out' sounds like the jug emptying; it is R being removed from the jug.
explanation.definitionFit: Pitchblende is a dark ore of uranium, a naturally occurring rock substance mined for radium and uranium.

clue.text: Fashion establishment maybe exporting uniform socks?

indicators.note: to export is to send goods out, so this letter leaves the word

blocks.note: a fashion house such as Dior is a couture business
Uniform is the NATO radio alphabet word for U

explanation.surface: A designer label sending school uniforms and socks abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform' looks like clothing, which suits the surface, but it is a code word for a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Hose is an old word for stockings and socks, so the question mark admits socks are only one example.

clue.text: Dreadful curse poetic Brexiteer probably produced

indicators.note: something dreadful is a terrible mess, so the letters come out jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A campaigner for leaving the EU writes some terrible verse full of swearing.
explanation.walkthrough: A Brexiteer backed Britain leaving the European Union; 'probably' covers that not every one is a sceptic of Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: Supporters of Brexit generally distrusted the EU, so one is likely a doubter of European integration.

clue.text: Noted English evangelist in debt, apparently

indicators.note: being in something means enclosed by it, so the pair sits within

blocks.note: being in debt is being in the red, from red ink used for losses
E is the abbreviation for English
Mark is one of the four gospel writers

explanation.surface: A well-known English preacher who seems to owe money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noted' looks like an adjective for a famous evangelist, but it is the past tense of note, meaning said. The evangelists are Matthew, Mark, Luke and John.
explanation.definitionFit: To note something aloud is to comment on it, so noted in the past tense means commented or observed.

clue.text: Brown & his followers showing antics the nation gets up to?

blocks.note: the nation is the land, and the antics are its own, so the land's
capers are playful antics
surface padding: the antics a nation gets up to are simply its antics

explanation.surface: A party leader called Brown and his supporters show off the country's political tricks.
explanation.walkthrough: Brown looks like Gordon Brown, the Labour Prime Minister, but it is Capability Brown, the 18th-century English garden designer.
explanation.definitionFit: Capability Brown designed grand estate parks, and those who followed his methods were garden designers of the same trade.

clue.text: Lusty male penning line in Ancient Greek

indicators.note: to pen is to shut in an enclosure, so one piece encloses another
being in something means enclosed by it, so the pair sits within

blocks.note: Attic is the dialect of ancient Athens
he is the male pronoun
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A randy Greek man writing a line of verse in the old language.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lusty' suggests desire, but its older meaning is strong and vigorous. Attic Greek was the language of classical Athens.
explanation.definitionFit: Lusty can mean healthy and robust, and an athletic build is likewise strong, fit and vigorous.

clue.text: Bound beer casks regularly start to drip

indicators.note: doing something regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter is kept

blocks.note: to bound is to leap, to spring
ale is a type of beer
the second and fourth letters of casks

explanation.surface: Beer barrels, tied up with hoops, start to drip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' reads as tied up, describing the casks, but it is the verb meaning leap.
explanation.definitionFit: To spring a leak is the idiom for a container or boat developing a hole and beginning to let liquid out.

clue.text: Space traveller in the lead orbiting globe to reach zenith

indicators.note: to orbit something is to circle all the way round it, so it ends up enclosed

blocks.note: a comet travels through space
a leader is ahead
the round letter O stands for a globe or ball

explanation.surface: A space rocket pulls ahead, circling the Earth on its way to its highest point.
explanation.walkthrough: The traveller and the leading phrase sit together and circle the globe between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A crisis that comes to a head reaches its peak or climax, the highest point, as the zenith is the sky's highest point.

clue.text: Note prisoner on train

indicators.note: in a down answer, on means placed over the top of the next piece

blocks.note: a con is a convict
a train of events is a sequence

explanation.surface: A note smuggled to an inmate on the railway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' looks like a written message, but it means importance, as in 'a person of note'.
explanation.definitionFit: A person of note is a person of consequence: both words mean importance or standing.

clue.text: Butcher in tie almost getting commendation

indicators.note: to butcher is to hack apart, so the letters are chopped up and reassembled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A butcher in a tie nearly wins praise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' looks like a signal to drop a letter, but it is part of the letters; 'Butcher' looks like a person, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A testimonial is a written statement praising someone's character or work, which is a commendation.

clue.text: Landlord’s requirement produces a tear

blocks.note: first meaning: the regular payment a tenant owes
second meaning: a rip

explanation.surface: Demands for money from a landlord make a tenant cry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear' reads as a drop from the eye, but it rhymes with bear: a rip.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenants pay a landlord rent; separately, a rent is an old word for a split or rip in cloth.

clue.text: Escort taking tea with former president

blocks.note: cha or char is British slang for tea
Juan Perón was president of Argentina

explanation.surface: A bodyguard having tea with an ex-head of state.
explanation.walkthrough: Cha is an old British word for tea, from Chinese. Perón led Argentina twice, alongside his wife Eva, 'Evita'.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaperon accompanies a young person to supervise them, which is to escort them.

clue.text: Small bird from Ireland nesting in old hat

indicators.note: a nesting bird settles inside its nest, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: passé means out of date, old hat
Erin is a poetic name for Ireland

explanation.surface: A little Irish bird has built its nest in a battered old hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old hat' is an idiom for out of date, not a real hat.
explanation.definitionFit: Passerines are perching songbirds such as sparrows and finches, most of them small.

clue.text: Control time off outside school

indicators.note: being outside something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: a rest is time off work
to school someone is to train them

explanation.surface: Keeping order on days off outside the school gates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School' looks like a noun, but it is the verb meaning teach or drill.
explanation.definitionFit: Restraint is self-control or a check on behaviour, so it is the act of holding something in check.

clue.text: Yankee dogging Ursula & Co moving noisily

indicators.note: moving letters around changes their order
a dog that dogs someone follows close behind, so this piece comes after

blocks.note: the name plus CO, the abbreviation for company
Yankee is the NATO radio alphabet word for Y

explanation.surface: An American tailing a woman and her friends as they move off loudly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yankee' looks like an American, but it is the radio code word for Y; '& Co' is the abbreviation for company.
explanation.definitionFit: Raucous means harsh and loud, so doing something raucously means doing it loudly and rowdily.

clue.text: Pipes drawn primarily by artist when older?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter counts
by means next to, so the pieces sit side by side

blocks.note: the first letter of drawn
RA is a Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts
in age, meaning in later years

explanation.surface: Smoking pipes sketched by a painter in later life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pipes' looks like tobacco pipes, which suits an old artist, but it means drains. The question mark flags the loose phrase 'in age'.
explanation.definitionFit: Drainage is the system of drains and sewers carrying water away, so it is a building's pipework.

clue.text: President‘s cleaner receiving one for each child

indicators.note: receiving something means taking it in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a char is a British word for a cleaning lady
the Roman numeral I is one
per means for each, as in miles per hour
a son is a child

explanation.surface: The president's housekeeper gets one each for the children.
explanation.walkthrough: A char, or charwoman, is an old British term for a cleaning lady.
explanation.definitionFit: The president of a committee or board is the person who presides over meetings, the chair.

clue.text: Fitting finale for player entering centre court

indicators.note: entering a place means going inside it, so this letter goes within
a finale is the closing part, so only the last letter is used

blocks.note: the core is the centre
the last letter of player
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A tennis player walks onto Centre Court for a fitting end to the match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Centre court' looks like Wimbledon's main court, but the words split into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Fitting behaviour is proper or appropriate, and correct conduct is likewise right and suitable.

clue.text: Aussie runners carrying flag round retired with honour

indicators.note: turned round means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards
carrying something means holding it inside, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: emus are flightless Australian birds that run fast
to flag is to grow weary, to tire

explanation.surface: Australian athletes run a lap with a flag after a winning career.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runners' looks like athletes and 'flag' like a banner, but they are birds and the verb meaning grow weary.
explanation.definitionFit: An emeritus professor has retired but keeps the title as an honour in recognition of long service.

clue.text: Florid men serving up limitless drink

without its limit means its end is cut off, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: OR is other ranks, the ordinary soldiers
cocoa is a hot chocolate drink

explanation.walkthrough: 'Florid' looks like red-faced, which suits the men, but it means elaborately decorated.
explanation.definitionFit: Rococo is the ornate 18th-century style of curls and scrollwork, so it is florid in the sense of over-decorated.

clue.text: Winged beast very excitedly going in two directions

indicators.note: something excited is stirred up, so the letters are thrown into a new order
going in means entering, so one piece is placed inside another

blocks.note: W for west and N for north, compass points
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Very' seems to qualify 'excitedly', but it is the letters to be stirred.
explanation.definitionFit: A wyvern is a heraldic dragon with two legs and wings, so it is a mythical flying creature.

clue.text: Is stopping army corps completely necessary?

blocks.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a corps of the British Army
quite means completely, as in quite right
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' looks like the verb starting a question, but it is the letters to be put inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A requisite thing is required for a purpose, so it means needed or necessary.

clue.text: Medicinal compound removing pressure from a swelling

indicators.note: removing means taking away, so this letter leaves the word

blocks.note: P is the symbol for pressure in physics
a lump is a swelling

explanation.surface: A drug that takes the pressure off a swollen lump.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the compound treat the swelling; in fact the swelling simply loses one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Alum is a mineral salt used as an astringent and styptic to stop bleeding, so it is a chemical used in medicine.

clue.text: Religious verse from old ledger ancient mistress gets hold of

indicators.note: getting hold of something means gripping it, so one piece clasps the other inside

blocks.note: doxy is an archaic word for a mistress
O is the abbreviation for old
a log is a record book, a ledger

explanation.surface: A hymn copied from an old account book that a former lover got her hands on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ancient mistress' sounds like a former lover, but it marks an archaic word: doxy.
explanation.definitionFit: A doxology is a short hymn of praise to God, such as the Gloria, sung at the end of psalms.

clue.text: Crookedly endorse last thirteen letters?

blocks.note: first meaning: to encourage or support wrongdoing

explanation.walkthrough: Thirteen is half of the 26 letters, so the last thirteen are the alphabet's back half; take the back half of the word alphabet instead.
explanation.definitionFit: To aid and abet is to help a criminal, so the verb means supporting someone in dishonest acts.

clue.text: Prophet and priest leading pilgrimage to west, taking day off

off means taken away, so this letter is removed
in an across answer west is leftward, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: Eli is the priest who raised Samuel in the Old Testament
the hadj, or hajj, is the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca
D is the abbreviation for day

explanation.surface: A holy man and a cleric set off westward on pilgrimage after taking a day's leave.
explanation.walkthrough: The pilgrimage is spelt HADJ here, one accepted form of hajj, so losing D leaves three letters to turn round.
explanation.definitionFit: Elijah is a major Old Testament seer who challenged the priests of Baal, a biblical prophet.

clue.text: Hellish collection of brief adornments I must appear in

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A set of skimpy decorations that I must turn up in, which is torture.

explanation.definitionFit: Fire and brimstone is the Bible's picture of the torments of damnation, so it describes something of the underworld.

clue.text: Levied tax on journalist’s last article in papers

being in something means enclosed by it, so this piece sits within

ID is identity documents, papers
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: A tax charged on the final piece a reporter wrote for the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Papers' looks like newspapers, which suits the journalist, but it means identity documents.
explanation.definitionFit: A tithe was a tenth of produce paid to the Church, so to tithe people was to charge them that levy.

clue.text: Cook takes pie in worst condition

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: Peaky is British slang for pale and unwell, so the most peaky person is in the worst health.

clue.text: Was prone to give up

blocks.note: first meaning: past tense of lie down, to be stretched out flat
second meaning: to surrender

explanation.surface: Someone who was always inclined to quit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Was prone to' reads as 'tended to'; split it, and 'prone' means lying face down.
explanation.definitionFit: Lay is the past of lie, so someone lying flat lay down; and to lay down weapons is to surrender them.
